summary.text: At \(k=2\), the binomial formulas show that every summand of the second tail is \(16=(2!)^4\) times the corresponding summand of the first. The first tail converges and is strictly positive (in particular, its \(n=3\) term is positive), so the two sums cannot be equal.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
U_k=\sum_{n\ge k+1}\frac{1}{n^3\prod_{j=1}^k(n^2-j^2)^2}
\]
and
\[
V_k=\sum_{n\ge k+1}
\frac{1}{n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}k^2(n-k)^2}.
\]
The conjecture asserts, in particular, that \(U_k=V_k\) for every integer \(k\ge 1\). We show that this first asserted equality already fails when \(k=2\). Consequently, no consideration of the further asserted equality involving \(\zeta(3)\), \(A281820\), and \(A281821\) is needed.

For context, the source of the failure is a missing factorial factor. For any \(n\ge k+1\), the standard product formulas for the binomial coefficients give
\[
\binom nk=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}
=\frac{\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(n-j)}{k!}
\]
and
\[
\binom{n+k}{k}=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)\cdots(n+k)}{k!}
=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^k(n+j)}{k!}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}k^2(n-k)^2\\
&\quad=\frac{n}{(k!)^4}
 \left(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(n-j)\right)^2
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^k(n+j)\right)^2(n-k)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adjoining the factor \(n-k\) to the first product and separating its initial factor \(n\), we have
\[
\left(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(n-j)\right)^2(n-k)^2
=\left(\prod_{j=0}^{k}(n-j)\right)^2
=n^2\left(\prod_{j=1}^k(n-j)\right)^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
 n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}k^2(n-k)^2
 &=\frac{n^3}{(k!)^4}
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^k(n-j)\right)^2
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^k(n+j)\right)^2\\
 &=\frac{n^3}{(k!)^4}\prod_{j=1}^k(n^2-j^2)^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \((n-j)(n+j)=n^2-j^2\). All these factors are nonzero for \(n\ge k+1\), so taking reciprocals is legitimate. Thus the summands satisfy the pointwise relation
\[
\frac{1}{n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}k^2(n-k)^2}
=(k!)^4\frac{1}{n^3\prod_{j=1}^k(n^2-j^2)^2}.
\]
For \(k=2\), the factor is \((2!)^4=16\).

We now give the specialization explicitly. For every \(n\ge3\), put
\[
u_n=\frac{1}{n^3(n^2-1)^2(n^2-4)^2}
\]
and
\[
v_n=\frac{1}{n\binom n2^2\binom{n+2}2^2(n-2)^2}.
\]
Using
\[
\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2,
\qquad
\binom{n+2}2=\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}2,
\]
we calculate the denominator of \(v_n\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
 n\binom n2^2\binom{n+2}2^2(n-2)^2
 &=n\left(\frac{n(n-1)}2\right)^2
      \left(\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}2\right)^2(n-2)^2\\
 &=\frac1{16}n^3(n-1)^2(n+1)^2(n-2)^2(n+2)^2\\
 &=\frac1{16}n^3(n^2-1)^2(n^2-4)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
v_n=16u_n                                                    \tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\ge3\).

It remains to ensure that the infinite sums can be compared and that the first one is not zero. Every \(u_n\) is positive. Moreover, when \(n\ge3\), both \((n^2-1)^2\) and \((n^2-4)^2\) are at least \(1\). Therefore
\[
0<u_n\le \frac1{n^3}.
\]
The series \(\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}1/n^3\) converges, so the comparison test shows that
\[
S:=\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}u_n
\]
converges. It is strictly positive: all of its terms are nonnegative, and already
\[
u_3=\frac{1}{3^3(3^2-1)^2(3^2-4)^2}
=\frac{1}{27\cdot64\cdot25}
=\frac1{43200}>0.
\]
Thus \(S\ge u_3>0\).

Equation (1) also shows that \(\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}v_n\) converges. Indeed, for every finite upper limit \(N\ge3\),
\[
\sum_{n=3}^N v_n=16\sum_{n=3}^N u_n.
\]
Passing to the limits of these partial sums gives
\[
V_2=\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}v_n
=16\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}u_n
=16S,
\]
whereas \(U_2=S\).

If the conjecture were true, its first equality at \(k=2\) would give \(U_2=V_2\). The preceding identities would then imply
\[
S=16S,
\]
so \(15S=0\), and hence \(S=0\). This contradicts \(S\ge1/43200>0\).

Therefore \(U_2\ne V_2\). Since the conjecture claims their equality for every \(k\ge1\), this single counterexample at \(k=2\) disproves the conjecture, irrespective of the additional claimed formula involving the numerator and denominator of Gosper’s partial sum.
